# The big picture {#sec-big-picture}

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll be able to do"}
Explain, in plain words, what the EvoDemo-Hyper MPM adds to an ordinary matrix population model,
and name the four vital rates and the genetic quantities the model tracks.
:::

## Two ways of thinking about change

When a population meets a changing environment, two research communities reach for different tools.

**Demographers** describe a population as numbers of individuals in *stages* — juveniles, adults —
and project them forward with a **matrix population model (MPM)**. This captures the life cycle
beautifully but, in its classic form, has no genetics: it cannot let a trait *evolve*.

**Evolutionary quantitative geneticists** describe a *trait* — its mean, its heritable (additive
genetic) variance — and predict its response to selection with the **breeder's equation**. This
captures evolution but tends to flatten the life cycle into a single "generation".

These two approaches have often led to different conclusions about the pace and consequences of
adaptation because they emphasise different biological processes [@vandewalle2025]. The
EvoDemo-Hyper MPM brings these perspectives together by combining a full demographic life cycle with
the dynamics of a heritable trait within a single matrix framework that remains computationally
efficient and transparent to analyse.

::: {.callout-tip title="Key idea"}
The EvoDemo-Hyper MPM is an ordinary matrix model with **two extra dimensions bolted on**: besides
*stage*, every individual also carries a **breeding value** (its heritable genetic contribution) and
a **phenotype**. Selection reshapes the trait distribution; inheritance passes it to offspring.
:::

## The life cycle

Everything in this workshop rests on one simple, two-stage life cycle: **juveniles (J)** and
**adults (A)**, censused just before breeding, with annual time steps.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  J(("Juvenile<br/>J")) -->|"S_J · γ — mature"| A(("Adult<br/>A"))
  J -->|"S_J · (1−γ) — stay J"| J
  A -->|"S_A — survive"| A
  A -->|"F — reproduce"| J
```
:::

Four **vital rates** govern the transitions:

- $S_J$ — juvenile survival,
- $S_A$ — adult survival,
- $\gamma$ — the probability a surviving juvenile matures into an adult,
- $F$ — fertility, the per-capita number of juveniles an adult contributes next year ($F = f \times S_J$).

Stacked into a projection matrix, the demography is just a $2\times2$ Leslie matrix:

$$
\mathbf{A} =
\begin{pmatrix}
S_J(1-\gamma) & F \\[2pt]
S_J\,\gamma   & S_A
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

That is the *entire* demographic skeleton. The five species you will meet later differ only in the
numbers that fill these four slots.

## Adding genetics

Now give every individual a quantitative trait $z$ that influences one of the vital rates. Following
the classic decomposition, the phenotype is a population mean plus a heritable **breeding value** and
an **environmental deviation**:

$$
z = \bar{z} + a + e, \qquad V_P = V_A + V_E, \qquad h^2 = \frac{V_A}{V_P}.
$$

Here $V_P$ is the phenotypic variance, $V_A$ the additive genetic variance, and $h^2$ the
**heritability** — the fraction of trait variation that is passed on. Selection acts on $z$; only the
breeding value $a$ is inherited.

The model discretises both the breeding value and the phenotype into a grid of classes (centred on
zero, spanning $\pm$ a range you choose). So instead of tracking "how many juveniles and adults",
it tracks **how many individuals of each (stage, breeding value, phenotype) combination** — a
three-dimensional *hyperstate*. Offspring draw their breeding value from their parents via the Fisher
infinitesimal model, which is how evolution enters.

You do not need the matrix algebra to use the model — we open that engine in
@sec-under-the-hood. For now, hold on to this:

::: {.callout-tip title="The model in one sentence"}
Project individuals through a structured life cycle while tracking the distribution of breeding
values and phenotypes, allowing selection, inheritance, and demography to operate simultaneously
within a single matrix framework.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Your turn — make a prediction"}
A fast-living grass and a slow-living albatross face the *same* selection pressure on the *same*
heritable trait. Which one do you expect to adapt **faster per year**? Write your guess down —
we will test it in @sec-slow-fast, and the answer is more interesting than it looks.
:::
